title: An Island's Running Balance
paragraphs: Any naturalist who has worked on islands knows two rules of thumb: large islands hold more species than small ones, and remote islands hold fewer than islands near a coast.

The first rule was given mathematical shape in 1921 by the Swedish botanist Olof Arrhenius, who found that species number rises with area as a power law: the count is proportional to area raised to a fixed exponent.
For true islands that exponent usually falls between about 0.2 and 0.35, which means that multiplying an island's area by ten roughly doubles its number of species.
Ecologists call this the species-area relationship, and for four decades it remained a description without a mechanism: it said what islands held, not why.
The why arrived in 1963, in a paper in the journal Evolution by Robert MacArthur and Edward O. Wilson, and in fuller form in their 1967 book, The Theory of Island Biogeography.

Wilson was a Harvard entomologist who had spent years collecting ants on islands of the western Pacific; MacArthur, at Princeton, was a mathematically minded ecologist who would die of cancer in 1972 at the age of 42.
Their shared idea was simple enough to sketch on a napkin: the number of species on an island is not a fixed property but a running balance between arrival and loss.
Immigration, in the theory's special sense, is the rate at which species from a mainland source pool arrive on an island where they are not already present.
That rate is highest at the start and falls as the island fills, because the pool of absent species shrinks and because the best dispersers tend to arrive first.
Extinction is the rate at which resident species disappear, and it rises as the island fills, because there are more species to lose and each has a smaller population.
Plot the falling immigration curve and the rising extinction curve against the number of species present, and the two lines cross.
MacArthur and Wilson called the species number at that crossing the equilibrium, and argued that every island drifts toward its own.
The elegance of the model lies in what it does with the two old rules of thumb.

Distance pulls the immigration curve down, since fewer colonists survive a long crossing; area pulls the extinction curve down, since a large island supports large populations that are hard to wipe out.
Four combinations follow: a large island near the mainland holds the most species, a small island far from it holds the fewest, and the other two cases fall between.
The species-area relationship stops being a bare description and becomes a consequence.
More striking, the model predicts that an island at equilibrium is not at rest: species keep arriving and keep vanishing at matching rates, so the roster turns over while the total stays put.
That last claim, turnover, is the part of the theory I find most impressive, because it was a risky prediction.
A theory that merely said big islands are rich could never be wrong.
A theory that said the names on an island's list should change from census to census, while the list's length held steady, could be checked, and could fail.

MacArthur and Wilson leaned on the record from Krakatau, the Indonesian volcanic island that erupted in 1883 and was left all but lifeless: over the following decades the number of resident bird species climbed and then leveled off while individual species kept coming and going.
A record kept by chance is not an experiment, and in 1966 Wilson and his graduate student Daniel Simberloff set out to run one.
Their islands were small clumps of red mangrove off the Florida Keys, each rooted in shallow water and small enough to be covered by a tent.
Mangrove islets suited the purpose because their animals were almost entirely arthropods, insects, spiders, and their relatives, which colonize quickly and can be counted on a few trees.
Simberloff censused every species on each islet, then hired a pest-control crew to tent the islet and fumigate it with methyl bromide, the method then used to rid houses of termites.
The islets came out nearly empty of animal life but structurally intact, so the experiment had changed nothing except the species count.
Over the next two years Simberloff returned repeatedly to record what had come back.
The results, published in the journal Ecology in 1969, fit the model better than anyone had a right to expect.
Within roughly a year, the number of species on most islets had climbed back to about its pre-fumigation level.
Islets closer to a source of colonists refilled faster and reached higher counts, while the most isolated islet lagged and settled below its original number.
The lists themselves were different: many returning species were not the ones that had been killed, and the membership kept shifting from visit to visit even after the totals had stabilized.
Here was turnover, observed rather than inferred.
The experiment had its limits, and it is worth being candid about them: the islets were minute, the animals were arthropods only, and two years is a short time.
Later work added texture without overturning the frame.

In 1977 James Brown and Astrid Kodric-Brown pointed out that distance affects extinction as well: on a near island, a dwindling population is regularly topped up by fresh arrivals of its own species, an idea they called the rescue effect.
And not every island sits at an equilibrium at all.

In 1971 Brown had examined small mammals on isolated mountaintops in the Great Basin of the western United States, where cool forest survives above desert; with the desert impassable, immigration had effectively stopped since the last ice age, and the faunas were simply losing species, a one-way slide ecologists call relaxation.
Jared Diamond carried the theory out of the academy in 1975, arguing that a nature reserve surrounded by cleared land is an island too, and should be designed like one.

His rules are still reproduced in textbooks: a large reserve beats a small one, one large reserve beats several small ones of the same total area, reserves close together beat reserves far apart, a compact shape beats a long thin one, and corridors between reserves beat none.
The second rule set off a quarrel that ran for years and acquired its own acronym, SLOSS, for single large or several small.

Simberloff himself, writing with Lawrence Abele in 1976, objected that several small reserves spread across different habitats might together hold more species than one large block, and that the theory gave no clean verdict.

The largest experiment built to settle such questions began in 1979 north of Manaus, in the Brazilian Amazon, where Thomas Lovejoy arranged with ranchers clearing forest to leave standing patches of 1, 10, and 100 hectares.
The Biological Dynamics of Forest Fragments Project has followed those patches for more than four decades.

The small fragments lost species quickly, the understory birds that follow army ant swarms among the first to go, and their edges dried and brightened as wind and sun pushed in, until a 1-hectare patch was in effect all edge.

But the project also showed how a fragment differs from an islet: when cleared land around a patch grew back into young secondary forest, birds began to cross it, and the patch behaved as if it had moved closer to the mainland.
That last finding is the one I would keep in front of anyone tempted to treat the theory as a blueprint.

An island is bounded by water that no beetle can walk across; a fragment is bounded by pasture, roads, and regrowth, a matrix that is sometimes a wall and sometimes a bridge, and one that people can change.
The equilibrium model earns its place because it turned two rules of thumb into a mechanism and then survived a real test on real islands.
It does not follow that a reserve can be sized by an exponent.
The honest use of the theory is as a scaffold for sharper questions about area, isolation, and loss, not as a formula that answers them.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the exponent in the species-area relationship for true islands implies that
choices: doubling an island's area roughly multiplies its species count by ten
a tenfold increase in island area roughly doubles the number of species
the number of species rises in direct proportion to an island's area
remote islands hold about one third as many species as islands near a coast
species number stops rising once an island exceeds a certain area

proof.quote: multiplying an island's area by ten roughly doubles its number of species

questions.why: Paragraph 1 says the exponent usually sits between about 0.2 and 0.35, which means that multiplying an island's area by ten roughly doubles its number of species. Ten times the area, twice the species.
distractorNotes: Reversed: the passage multiplies area by ten and gets twice the species, not the other way around.
Contradicted: a power law with an exponent well below one is not direct proportion; ten times the area gives only twice the species.
Mash-up: 0.35 is the upper end of the exponent, and the remoteness rule in paragraph 1 has no number attached.
Outside the passage: nothing says the species count ever stops rising with area.

questions.stem: The passage states which of the following about Robert MacArthur?
choices: He spent years collecting ants on islands of the western Pacific.
He published the equilibrium theory alone in 1963 before Wilson joined him.
He was a Harvard entomologist with a gift for field collecting.
He was a mathematically minded ecologist who worked at Princeton.
He fumigated mangrove islets in the Florida Keys with Simberloff.

proof.quote: MacArthur, at Princeton, was a mathematically minded ecologist

questions.why: Paragraph 2 places MacArthur at Princeton and calls him a mathematically minded ecologist, in contrast to Wilson the Harvard entomologist.
distractorNotes: Wrong person: paragraph 2 gives the ant collecting to Wilson.
Contradicted: paragraph 2 says the 1963 paper was by MacArthur and Wilson together.
Wrong person: Wilson was the Harvard entomologist.
Wrong person: paragraph 6 says Wilson and his student Simberloff ran the fumigation experiment.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the immigration rate falls as an island fills because
choices: fewer absent species remain and the best dispersers have already arrived
the resident species crowd out newcomers through sharper competition
the mainland source pool itself shrinks as species leave it for the island
each resident species has a smaller population and is easier to lose
longer crossings become necessary once the nearest sources are used up

proof.quote: because the pool of absent species shrinks and because the best dispersers tend to arrive first

questions.why: Paragraph 3 gives two reasons the immigration rate falls: the pool of species still absent from the island shrinks, and the best dispersers tend to arrive first, leaving slower travelers for later.
distractorNotes: Outside the passage: competition among residents is never offered as a reason for falling immigration.
Misread: the pool that shrinks is the set of species not yet on the island; the passage never says the mainland loses species.
Wrong process: a smaller population per species is paragraph 3's reason that extinction rises, not that immigration falls.
Outside the passage: nothing is said about crossings growing longer as an island fills.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that if an island's extinction curve were lowered while its immigration curve stayed the same, the island's equilibrium number of species would
choices: fall, because fewer new species would arrive to replace those that were lost
stay the same, because the equilibrium depends only on immigration
fall, because the two curves would no longer cross at any point
stay the same, because turnover holds the total fixed regardless
rise, because the curves would cross at a higher species count

proof.quote: called the species number at that crossing the equilibrium
area pulls the extinction curve down, since a large island supports large populations that are hard to wipe out
a large island near the mainland holds the most species

questions.why: Paragraph 3 defines the equilibrium as the crossing of the two curves, and paragraph 4 says a large island pulls the extinction curve down and holds more species. Lowering the extinction curve moves the crossing to a higher species count.
distractorNotes: Reversed: the immigration curve is unchanged, and a lower extinction curve means fewer losses, not fewer arrivals.
Contradicted: paragraph 3 makes the equilibrium depend on both curves, which is why area matters in paragraph 4.
Contradicted: a lower extinction curve still rises as the island fills, so it still crosses the falling immigration curve.
Wrong idea: turnover in paragraph 4 describes what happens at a given equilibrium, not what sets its size.

questions.stem: The author mentions Krakatau in paragraph 5 primarily to
choices: show that volcanic islands recover their species faster than other islands
describe the method that Simberloff and Wilson would later copy
point to a real-world record that bore out the turnover prediction
argue that bird species are better dispersers than arthropods
demonstrate that the species-area relationship fails on remote islands

proof.quote: could be checked, and could fail
the number of resident bird species climbed and then leveled off while individual species kept coming and going

questions.why: Paragraph 5 sets up turnover as a prediction that could be checked, then says MacArthur and Wilson leaned on the Krakatau record, where the bird count leveled off while individual species kept coming and going. Krakatau is there as evidence for turnover.
distractorNotes: Outside the passage: no comparison of recovery speed between volcanic and other islands is made.
Contradicted: paragraph 6 says a record kept by chance is not an experiment, and the islets were fumigated, not left to a volcano.
Outside the passage: birds and arthropods are never compared as dispersers.
Wrong idea: Krakatau illustrates turnover, not a failure of the species-area relationship.

questions.stem: According to the passage, mangrove islets were well suited to the experiment because
choices: their animals were mainly arthropods, which colonize fast and are easily counted
red mangroves regrow rapidly after fumigation strips them of their leaves and bark
they were the only islands near a mainland source pool of colonists
their arthropods were resistant to methyl bromide and survived fumigation
they had been censused by naturalists for decades before the study began

proof.quote: their animals were almost entirely arthropods, insects, spiders, and their relatives, which colonize quickly and can be counted on a few trees

questions.why: Paragraph 6 says the islets suited the purpose because their animals were almost entirely arthropods, which colonize quickly and can be counted on a few trees.
distractorNotes: Outside the passage: paragraph 6 says the islets came out structurally intact, and nothing is said about regrowth.
Too extreme and never said: the passage does not call them the only islands near a source.
Reversed: the fumigation left the islets nearly empty of animal life, so the arthropods did not survive it.
Wrong detail: the decades-long record belongs to Krakatau in paragraph 5; Simberloff did the censusing himself.

questions.stem: All of the following are stated in the passage about the Florida Keys experiment EXCEPT:
choices: The islets were fumigated with methyl bromide.
Simberloff counted every species on each islet before the fumigation.
Most islets regained roughly their earlier number of species within about a year.
The most isolated islet eventually exceeded its original species count.
Many of the species that returned differed from those that had been killed.

proof.quote: fumigate it with methyl bromide
Simberloff censused every species on each islet
Within roughly a year, the number of species on most islets had climbed back
many returning species were not the ones that had been killed
the most isolated islet lagged and settled below its original number

questions.why: Paragraph 7 says the most isolated islet lagged and settled below its original number, the opposite of exceeding it. The other four statements are all in paragraphs 6 and 7.
distractorNotes: Stated in paragraph 6: the crew tented each islet and fumigated it with methyl bromide.
Stated in paragraph 6: Simberloff censused every species on each islet, then hired the crew.
Stated in paragraph 7: within roughly a year most islets had climbed back to about their earlier level.
Stated in paragraph 7: many returning species were not the ones that had been killed.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 7, the word 'minute' most nearly means
choices: brief
tiny
exact
few
remote

proof.quote: the islets were minute

questions.why: Paragraph 7 lists the experiment's limits, and the first is that the islets were minute: paragraph 6 has already called them small clumps small enough to cover with a tent. The word here means very small, not a unit of time.
distractorNotes: This leans on the sixty-second meaning of the word; the sentence is about the islets' size, and the time limit is a separate item in the same list.
Minute can mean precise, as in a minute examination, but an islet cannot be exact; the sentence is about how small it is.
The sentence says nothing about how many islets there were; it describes each islet's size.
Isolation is discussed elsewhere in paragraph 7, but this word describes size, not distance.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the most isolated islet in the experiment
choices: was never fully emptied of animal life by the fumigation
refilled faster than the others because it faced less competition
reached a higher count than before because turnover added species
received colonists only after two years had passed
refilled more slowly and leveled off below its earlier number

proof.quote: the most isolated islet lagged and settled below its original number

questions.why: Paragraph 7 says islets closer to a source refilled faster and higher, while the most isolated islet lagged and settled below its original number.
distractorNotes: Wrong detail: paragraph 6 says the islets came out nearly empty, and no islet is singled out as an exception.
Reversed: paragraph 7 says the most isolated islet lagged behind the others.
Reversed: it settled below its original number, not above it.
Too extreme: the passage says it lagged, not that it received nothing for two years.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that, once the rescue effect is taken into account, an island near the mainland should
choices: receive fewer new species than a far island of the same size
have a higher extinction rate than a far island of the same size
lose resident species less often than a far island of the same size
reach equilibrium only after its dwindling populations have died out
hold the same number of species as a far island of the same size

proof.quote: distance affects extinction as well: on a near island, a dwindling population is regularly topped up by fresh arrivals of its own species

questions.why: Paragraph 8 says that on a near island a dwindling population is regularly topped up by fresh arrivals of its own species, so distance affects extinction too. A population that keeps getting topped up is harder to lose, which means fewer extinctions on the near island.
distractorNotes: Reversed: paragraph 4 says distance pulls immigration down, so the near island receives more new species, not fewer.
Reversed: the rescue effect lowers extinction on the near island.
Contradicted: the rescue effect keeps dwindling populations alive rather than waiting for them to die.
Contradicted: paragraphs 4 and 8 both give the near island more species, not the same number.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the mammal faunas on Great Basin mountaintops
choices: reached equilibrium soon after the last ice age ended
gain new species whenever the desert between peaks is crossed
were rescued from extinction by arrivals from nearby mountains
turned over steadily while their totals stayed roughly constant
were losing species with almost no immigration to replace them

proof.quote: immigration had effectively stopped since the last ice age, and the faunas were simply losing species

questions.why: Paragraph 8 says that with the desert impassable, immigration had effectively stopped since the last ice age and the faunas were simply losing species, a slide the passage calls relaxation.
distractorNotes: Contradicted: paragraph 8 introduces the mountaintops as islands that do not sit at an equilibrium.
Contradicted: the desert is described as impassable, so it is not being crossed.
Reversed: the rescue effect in paragraph 8 belongs to near islands, and these mountaintops get no arrivals.
Wrong idea: turnover with a steady total is the equilibrium pattern of paragraph 4, which these faunas do not show.

questions.stem: The author lists Diamond's reserve design rules in paragraph 9 primarily to
choices: show how the theory was turned into practical guidance for reserves
endorse the rules as the best available method for sizing a reserve
prove that Simberloff had abandoned the theory he had once helped to test
explain why the Amazon fragments were cut to 1, 10, and 100 hectares
demonstrate that the species-area exponent applies to cleared land

proof.quote: a nature reserve surrounded by cleared land is an island too, and should be designed like one
The second rule set off a quarrel

questions.why: Paragraph 9 opens with Diamond carrying the theory out of the academy and arguing that a reserve should be designed like an island; the rules are the concrete form that guidance took, and the quarrel that follows grows out of one of them.
distractorNotes: Too strong: the author reports that the rules are still reproduced in textbooks, then immediately turns to the quarrel over one of them, which is not an endorsement.
Outside the passage: paragraph 9 says Simberloff objected to one rule, not that he abandoned the theory.
Wrong paragraph: the fragment sizes in paragraph 10 are never tied to Diamond's rules.
Outside the passage: the exponent appears in paragraph 1 for true islands, and paragraph 11 doubts it can size a reserve.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that Simberloff's view of the equilibrium theory was that it
choices: had failed its test on the mangrove islets and should be set aside
proved that a single large reserve always outperforms several small ones
applied to arthropods on islets but never to birds or mammals
held up on islets but did not settle how reserves should be built
was sound in principle but had never been tested in the field

proof.quote: fit the model better than anyone had a right to expect
the theory gave no clean verdict

questions.why: Paragraph 7 says Simberloff's own results fit the model better than anyone expected, and paragraph 9 says that in the reserve debate he objected that the theory gave no clean verdict. Put together, he saw it confirmed on islets but not as a ruling on reserve design.
distractorNotes: Contradicted: paragraph 7 says the results fit the model unusually well.
Reversed: paragraph 9 says Simberloff objected to the one-large rule.
Too extreme and never said: the passage lists arthropods as a limit of the experiment, not as the theory's boundary.
Contradicted: Simberloff ran the field test himself, as paragraphs 6 and 7 describe.

questions.stem: According to the passage, each of the following is true of the Biological Dynamics of Forest Fragments Project EXCEPT:
choices: It began in 1979 north of Manaus in the Brazilian Amazon.
Its patches were cut in sizes of 1, 10, and 1,000 hectares.
Understory birds that follow army ant swarms were among the first species lost.
It has followed its forest patches for more than four decades.
Birds began crossing cleared land once secondary forest grew back.

proof.quote: began in 1979 north of Manaus, in the Brazilian Amazon
the understory birds that follow army ant swarms among the first to go
has followed those patches for more than four decades
when cleared land around a patch grew back into young secondary forest, birds began to cross it
patches of 1, 10, and 100 hectares

questions.why: Paragraph 10 gives the patch sizes as 1, 10, and 100 hectares; the largest is 100, not 1,000. Every other statement is in paragraph 10.
distractorNotes: Stated in paragraph 10: the experiment began in 1979 north of Manaus, in the Brazilian Amazon.
Stated in paragraph 10: the understory birds that follow army ant swarms were among the first to go.
Stated in paragraph 10: the project has followed the patches for more than four decades.
Stated in paragraph 10: once cleared land grew back into young secondary forest, birds began to cross it.

questions.stem: Which new situation best illustrates the point the author draws from the Amazon fragments in paragraphs 10 and 11?
choices: A pond that dries up each summer loses its fish and is restocked every spring by a state hatchery
A mountaintop forest keeps losing species because the desert around it cannot be crossed
A city park gains new butterfly species after nearby lots are planted with wildflowers
An offshore island gains species when a larger island nearby is set aside as a reserve
A small reserve holds fewer bird species than a large reserve of the same shape

proof.quote: when cleared land around a patch grew back into young secondary forest, birds began to cross it, and the patch behaved as if it had moved closer to the mainland
a matrix that is sometimes a wall and sometimes a bridge, and one that people can change

questions.why: Paragraph 10 says that when the land around a fragment grew back, birds crossed it and the fragment behaved as if it were closer to its source, and paragraph 11 calls that surrounding matrix a wall or a bridge that people can change. A park that gains species once its surroundings become crossable is the same pattern.
distractorNotes: Wrong mechanism: the hatchery delivers the fish directly; nothing about the pond's surroundings has become easier to cross.
Wrong paragraph: this is the relaxation case from paragraph 8, where the matrix stays a wall.
Wrong mechanism: the water between the islands is unchanged, so the island has not become easier to reach.
Wrong rule: this illustrates the area effect, not the idea that the surrounding matrix can change.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward using the equilibrium theory as a blueprint for reserve design is best described as
choices: admiring
hostile
indifferent
cautious
bewildered

proof.quote: anyone tempted to treat the theory as a blueprint
It does not follow that a reserve can be sized by an exponent.
not as a formula that answers them

questions.why: Paragraph 11 warns anyone tempted to treat the theory as a blueprint, says a reserve cannot be sized by an exponent, and offers the theory as a scaffold for questions rather than a formula. That is a careful, hedging voice, not a dismissive or an admiring one.
distractorNotes: Wrong target: the author admires the theory itself in paragraphs 5 and 11, but the question asks about using it as a blueprint, which the author warns against.
Too strong: paragraph 11 says the model earns its place and is a useful scaffold, so the author is not against it.
Too weak: the author takes a clear position and spends the final paragraph defending it.
Wrong register: the author explains the limits of the theory confidently, not in confusion.

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
choices: Simberloff's mangrove experiment proved that an island's species count never changes once its equilibrium has been reached
The equilibrium theory explained island species counts and passed a field test, but it is a guide to questions about fragments, not a formula
Nature reserves should always be designed as single large blocks because the island theory shows that large islands hold the most species
The species-area relationship is a dependable law that allows ecologists to predict exactly how many species a reserve of any size will hold
The Amazon fragments project overturned the equilibrium theory by showing that habitat fragments do not behave like true islands in any respect

proof.quote: a running balance between arrival and loss
it turned two rules of thumb into a mechanism and then survived a real test on real islands
a scaffold for sharper questions about area, isolation, and loss, not as a formula that answers them

questions.why: The passage explains the equilibrium theory, follows it through the Krakatau record and the mangrove experiment, then turns to reserves and fragments and closes by calling the theory a scaffold for questions rather than a formula. Only one choice covers both the theory's success and its limits.
distractorNotes: Reversed: paragraph 7 found turnover, meaning the membership kept changing; it was the total, not the list, that held steady.
Too extreme and contradicted: paragraph 9 says the single-large rule set off a quarrel and the theory gave no clean verdict.
Contradicted: paragraph 11 says it does not follow that a reserve can be sized by an exponent.
Too strong: paragraph 10 shows fragments differ from islets in one respect, but paragraph 11 still says the model earns its place.
